chapter.name: PythonTap Tutorial 2: A Filter That Knows the Sample Rate
chapter.header: PythonTap Tutorial 2: A Filter That Knows the Sample Rate
chapter.body: A gain needs nothing but its input. A filter remembers the samples before, and to turn a time in milliseconds or a frequency in hertz into samples it needs the sample rate. This tutorial uses allpass.py, a Schroeder allpass filter, to show both.
Open the tutorial patcher, and turn on the audio.

An optional method prepare(self, sample_rate: float, vector_size: int) -> None is called with Max's sample rate and signal vector size before the object processes any audio, again whenever either changes, and on every reload before the new code runs. allpass.py uses it to size its delay line, and prints what it did: look in the Max console for "Setting delay to 1.0 ms".

An allpass filter passes every frequency at the same level and shifts their phase: alone, it sounds like its input. Mixed with the dry signal, as in the patcher, the phase shifts cancel some frequencies and reinforce others. Change delay and alpha with the attrui objects and listen to the notches move.

The class's fields are attrs fields, and alpha has a validator: it must stay strictly between -1 and 1. Click alpha 1: the validator raises an exception, its traceback prints to the Max console, and alpha keeps the value it had. An exception in your code never takes Max down.

numpy_allpass.py computes exactly what allpass.py does — sample for sample — but a vector at a time, with numpy. Switch to it and compare the CPU meter: per sample, every line of the filter's Python runs once per sample; per vector, a few numpy expressions run once per vector.
Here is a one-pole lowpass filter, per sample, with its cutoff in hertz:

Save it as python/onepole.py and make a tap.python~ onepole object. Fields whose names start with an underscore are private: they are not attributes, so only cutoff appears in the inspector. Try computing a in prepare() and again only when cutoff changes, instead of on every sample.

prepare() tells the class the sample rate and vector size whenever they change. Its state lives in private fields, which start afresh on a reload — prepare() is called again before the new code runs — while its attributes keep their values, guarded by their validators.
